Finished
FIN-isht
v. (past part.)
From Latin finire, to end, from finis, an end or boundary. Webster 1828: ended; completed; perfected; polished to the highest degree. The word stands at three great terminals in Scripture — the finished creation, the finished work of Christ, and the finished course of a servant.

Biblical Definition

Finished marks completions, and Scripture places three of them where a reader cannot miss them. The first closes creation: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them (Genesis 2:1), and God rested, not from weariness but because the work was done. The second is the sixth word from the cross, and in the Greek it is a single word: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost (John 19:30). It is not a sigh of exhaustion but the merchant’s and the servant’s word for a debt discharged and a task completed. He had already said it to the Father in the upper room, in the past tense, before He went to Gethsemane: I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do (John 17:4). The third is Paul’s, from a Roman cell, with execution near: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). One finished work purchases salvation; the other finished course is the evidence of a life laid hold of by it, and the two must never be confused or the gospel is lost.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FINISHED as ended, completed, perfected, and adds the sense of being polished to the highest degree of excellence — as a finished performance. Both senses are present in It is finished: the work ended, and nothing wanting in it.

expand to see more

FINISHED, pp. — Ended; completed; done; perfected.

Polished to the highest degree of excellence; as a finished poem, a finished education.

FINISH, v.t. — To arrive at the end of, in performance; to complete; to bring to an end.

To perfect; to bestow the last touches on; to render complete and excellent.

The commercial force of the Greek behind John 19:30 — a debt marked paid in full — is not conveyed by any single English word, but Webster’s completed and perfected together come near it.

Key Scripture

Genesis 2:1 — "Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them."

John 17:4 — "I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do."

John 19:30 — "When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost."

2 Timothy 4:7 — "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:"

Hebrews 10:14 — "For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified."

Modern Corruption

Every religion of human merit is a denial that the work is finished, and so is every Protestant conscience that keeps re-opening a settled account — Rome’s continuing sacrifice on one side, and the believer’s habit of re-crucifying Christ in his own guilt on the other.

expand to see more

The Roman mass is defined as a true and proper propitiatory sacrifice offered for the living and the dead, and the Reformers judged it a denial of John 19:30 for that reason. Hebrews argues at length that the levitical priests stood daily offering the same sacrifices which can never take away sins, but that this Man, after He had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down. Sitting is the posture the argument turns on; there was no seat in the tabernacle because the priest’s work was never done. By one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. Purgatory, indulgences, the treasury of merit, and the continuing sacrifice all rest on the assumption that something remains to be paid, and the single Greek word from the cross is the answer to all four.

The Protestant version of the same error is quieter and troubles more consciences. A believer who accepts justification by faith alone as a doctrine may still live as though today’s failure re-opened the account, and treat his assurance as rising and falling with his performance. The remedy is not to think less of the failure but to think more of the finishing. Christ said It is finished before He gave up the ghost, and He said I have finished the work before Gethsemane, and the resurrection was the Father’s receipt. Paul’s I have finished my course belongs to a different order entirely: it is the fruit of the first finishing, not a contribution to it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek teleo (G5055), to bring to an end, to complete, to pay; the perfect tetelestai at John 19:30; Hebrew kalah (H3615), to be complete, at Genesis 2:1.

expand to see more

Greek teleo (G5055) — to finish, complete, accomplish, and in commercial use to pay in full.

Greek tetelestai — the perfect passive at John 19:30: it has been finished and stands finished.

Greek teleioo (G5048) — to perfect, to bring to the goal; I have finished the work (John 17:4).

Greek dromos (G1408) — a course, a race-track; I have finished my course (2 Timothy 4:7).

Hebrew kalah (H3615) — to be complete, to be at an end; the heavens and the earth were finished (Genesis 2:1).

Usage

"Thus the heavens and the earth were finished (Genesis 2:1) — the first completion, followed by rest."

"It is finished (John 19:30) — one Greek word, a debt discharged."

"I have finished my course (2 Timothy 4:7) — the servant’s completion, which is fruit and not payment."
